newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin illness renews concern about stability.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin illness renews concern about stability.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's admission to hospital with the first signs of pneumonia has renewed concern that Russia could become dangerously rudderless and unstable in his absence.

The 65-year-old president's return to hospital on Wednesday only two months after heart surgery was quickly seized on by one of his political foes, who questioned his ability to govern and urged him to step down for the good of the country.

But the experience of the last year, when major upheavals were avoided despite Yeltsin's long absence from the Kremlin with heart problems, suggests fears of instability could yet be proved wrong -- at least in the short term.

"The political situation in Russia has already become pretty stable," Sergei Markov, a political analyst at the Moscow branch of the independent Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Reuters.
"The federal government, the prime minister and the head of the presidential staff, Anatoly Chubais, can definitely control the situation."

Chubais, the chief of the Kremlin administration, and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, the president's constitutional understudy, took over the running of the country while Yeltsin was absent for the heart surgery which he had on November 5.
National security adviser Alexander Lebed also had a brief share of power but was sacked by Yeltsin on October 17 because of what the president said were his open presidential ambitions.
Lebed said before his dismissal that an army rebellion was imminent, the Kremlin was divided and reforms were mostly on hold.
But predictions of an autumn economic crisis, which would prompt protests by unpaid workers, proved wrong.
There were some protests but the army did not rebel and the opposition communists avoided outright confrontation.
Yeltsin may claim some responsiblity for maintaining relative stability by balancing rival interest groups in the Kremlin to prevent any single force gaining too much power.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin kept in touch with affairs of state while in hospital and even took all the major decisions.
But many analysts question whether Yeltsin was really able to play such a role and say that only proved Russia can get along without his close involvement in everyday political affairs.
"Even if Boris Yeltsin is sick and spends most of his time between hospital and his dacha (country residence), it will not influence Russian politics too much. It will stay stable," Markov said.
Other analysts disagree, saying instability cannot be ruled out in Russia, where democracy is young and the president has vast powers.
Critics suggest that although major disasters have been averted in the last few months, many problems have simply not been tackled properly and are therefore becoming more acute.
These include the problem of the wages owed to millions of workers in the public sector, some of whom have not been paid for several months despite government promises.
Lebed, who is a likely challenger in the next presidential election, lost no time in expressing his concern.
"Our country is headed by a very sick and elderly man. He needs to retire," he told Ekho Moskvy radio on Wednesday.

"In keeping with the constitution, our country is designed for one man, for the president. If the president is in hospital, everything stops. This should not be the case because the situation in our country is far too tense."
Such comments are unlikely to fall completely on deaf ears among the Russian public. They might even help revive the jostling for position which reached a peak last autumn.

"The events...give more credit to the persistent claims of General Lebed and the president's other political opponents that they have some exclusive information about his real state of health and that we will possibly have the next presidential election within the next couple of months," political analyst Andrei Piontkowski told the British Broadcatsing Corporation.

"I am suggesting that even if this disease is not very serious, it increases the political instability in this country and we are returning to the situation of October and November when there was a real presidential race between the would-be candidates."
